title: Candide, Voltaire
subject: litterature
description: Candide goes through a cruel world believing that everything is for the best. Voltaire demolishes Leibniz's optimism with implacable irony.

hero.hook: Thirty chapters, corrosive irony, and a final sentence that changes everything.

blocks.text: Published in **1759**, **Candide or Optimism** is the masterpiece of the philosophical tale, a short story combining adventure and reflection. **Voltaire**, whose real name is **François-Marie Arouet**, demolishes the idea of ​​a world perfectly ordered by providence, the will of God guiding everything.

In thirty quick chapters, the story belongs to the **[[The philosophy of the Enlightenment]]**, an 18th century movement based on reason and criticism of prejudice. Man must act concretely, not just speculate on the meaning of the world. Voltaire uses humor and exaggeration to make the reader think without lecturing them.

Voltaire wrote Candide after the **[[Seven Years' War]]**, the great European conflict from 1756 to 1763, and especially the earthquake of **Lisbon**, November 1 **1755**. Around 60, 000 people die on this religious holiday. How can we still believe that all evil serves a greater good?

blocks.caption: The Lisbon earthquake: a disaster that shatters confidence in a perfect world.

blocks.text: Voltaire attacks the . According to this philosophy, God created the best of all possible worlds. Any apparent evil would serve a greater good. Candide is born from this refusal. The philosophical tale combines light fiction and deep reflection to reach a wide audience, not just specialists. **[[Leibniz's optimism]]**

blocks.caption: Voltaire: irony, lucidity and fight for reason.

blocks.text: **Candid**, a naive young man, is raised in the castle of Baron **Thunder-ten-tronckh** by **Pangloss**, caricature of , a 17th century German philosopher. The tutor claims that every event, no matter how atrocious, has a beneficial cause in a divine plan. **[[Leibniz]]**
Despite the ban by the Parliament of Paris, the book circulated clandestinely: it is estimated that more than 20,000 copies were made in the first year.

Driven from his castle for having loved **Cunégonde**, the baron's daughter, the hero is confronted with the horrors of the world: forced enlistment in the army, the storm, illness and the **[[Inquisition]]**, an ecclesiastical tribunal which prosecuted heresy. The Inquisition practices the **[[Auto-da-fé]]**, a public ceremony where condemned people are sometimes burned, to prevent new earthquakes.

The absurdity culminates when Pangloss explains that syphilis is essential for chocolate. Voltaire forces the reader to reject abstract speculation to embrace lucid observation. Every catastrophe becomes a lesson in irony. The tale moves quickly, like a series of comic blows aimed at human stupidity.

sections.title: Eldorado and the Negro from Surinam

blocks.text: The **Eldorado**, an imaginary South American utopia, proves that optimism can hold in a rational and peaceful society. Yet Candide leaves her to find **Cunégonde**. Static perfection does not suit man: he wants to act, to love, to move. Voltaire suggests that happiness is not a state, but an activity.
This is the price you eat sugar for in Europe.
blocks.attribution: Voltaire, Candide — the Negro from Suriname

blocks.text: The **negro from Surinam**, a slave mutilated for European sugar, pushes Candide to define optimism: “it is the rage to maintain that everything is good when one is bad”. The parodic story of the coming-of-age novel, where a hero learns life through experience, forces the reader to make a lucid observation in the face of colonial injustices.

The outcome takes place in a Turkish small farm, with **Pangloss**, **Cunégonde** and other companions in misfortune. Candide concludes: “**We must cultivate our garden**”. No more metaphysical speculation about God and the meaning of the world: only concrete action counts. Voltaire refuses any global response to the evil of the world, but offers lucid pragmatism.
